newsitem.title: UK: Major's highs and lows since 1992 election.
newsitem.headline: Major's highs and lows since 1992 election.

text.p: John Major has lurched from one political crisis to another during his 6-1/2 years as prime minister and is now trailing in the polls for a May 1 election.
But he is no stranger to adversity, having come from behind to win the April 1992 general election.
Major replaced Margaret Thatcher at the head of the right-wing Conservative Party after an internal revolt unseated the "Iron Lady" in November 1990.
Here are his highs and lows since the last election:
September 1992 - Black Wednesday. Major pulls Britain out of Europe's exchange rate mechanism (ERM); Sterling collapses.
David Mellor resigns from the cabinet after allegations about his personal life. He is the first of many ministers and ministerial aides to quit under a cloud of "sleaze" and personal scandal.
May 1993 - Major sacks Chancellor Norman Lamont after series of gaffes compound ERM debacle. Lamont savages Major in parliament.
Conservatives lose Newbury by-election to minority Liberal Democrats, the first in a series of by-election losses that gradually whittle away his 21-seat majority.
July 1993 - Twenty-three Euro-sceptic Conservatives vote against government in key vote on Maastricht treaty; Major calls and wins vote of confidence on over-all European policy
January 1994 - Three scandal-hit ministers resign in a week, making a mockery of Major's "Back to Basics" call for a return to traditional morality.
June 1995 - Whispering campaign over chance of a leadership challenge; Major tells dissenters to "put up or shut up" and take him on in an open contest.
July 1995 - Major defeats party leadership challenge by right-wing Euro-sceptic challenger John Redwood.
October 1995 - Former minister Alan Howarth quits Conservatives to join opposition Labour Party, the first of four House of Commons defections.
January 1996 - Former premier Margaret Thatcher says the government should not throw away her achievements; her speech is seen as thinly veiled criticism of Major.
March 1996 - Scientists report that deadly "mad cow" disease may spread to humans who eat infected beef; EU ban on British beef exports takes relations with bloc to new low.
December 1996 - Major's majority finally disappears when Labour retains safe seat of Barnsley East. This leaves him at the mercy of Protestant Ulster Unionists in parliament.
March 17 - Major announces election will be held May 1.
